newsitem.title: FRANCE: French car sales tumble 33.6 percent in January.
newsitem.headline: French car sales tumble 33.6 percent in January.

text.p: New car sales in France slid 33.6 percent in January from artificially inflated levels a year earlier, the French carmakers association CCFA said on Monday.

It said the drop in new car sales to 122,552 last month from 184,541 in January, 1996, underscored the weakness in the market since the September 30 expiry of a year-long state rebate programme, which underpinned demand in January of last year.
The CCFA said the year-earlier figure was also boosted by a spurt in sales following the disruption caused by three weeks of public transport strikes in November and December of 1995.
A CCFA spokesman said January 1996 car sales were probably inflated by 20,000 units due to the spillover of 1995 orders.
"There's still a lack of dynamism in this market, but it's not as bad as the 33.6 percent drop suggests," said a spokeswoman for Renault SA.
Industry officials and experts predict French car sales will fall between eight and 10 percent this year from 1.93 million units in 1996 unless the government restores incentives.

"This is not a very good start to the year," said Salomon Brothers analyst John Lawson. "I've tried to pull out the abnormal factors and I reckon it was a 1.5 million to 1.6 million unit seasonally adjusted rate. This is the lowest monthly rate since January 1993."
French carmakers fared worse than foreign manufacturers, taking 53.4 percent of the domestic market last month, down from 55.7 percent in January 1996.

The best performers were Volvo, whose car sales were 23 percent above year-earlier levels, and General Motors' Opel subsidiary, which saw a 10.7 percent sales drop -- the smallest among Europe's Big Six mass producers.
PSA Peugeot Citroen car sales plunged 43 percent to 29,829, while Renault sales fell 29.3 percent to 35,622.
A spokeswoman at the Peugeot group said its sales were hurt because the company, struggling to preserve its profit margins, resisted price cuts until mid-January.
"We saw everyone doing aggressive promotions, and we joined on January 15," the spokeswoman told Reuters.
Carmakers are engaged in a fierce price war in the French market that is especially harmful to the French manufacturers, which rely on domestic sales for their biggest profits.

Although the French government ended the rebate scheme, some manufacturers including Ford and Fiat, are still offering discounts to buyers turning in old cars, and just about everyone is proposing some kind of deal for customers.
Industry officials are beginning to press the government for help, and a Fiat official recently said he thought the French government would revive the rebate scheme.
The last rebate scheme was introduced in October 1995 to boost the market, which was flagging after the expiry three months earlier of a prior rebate programme.
Sources at the Industry Ministry will say only that they are watching the market's evolution.
PSA shares were down 3.54 percent at 572 francs in afternoon trading, while Renault shares were 0.92 percent lower at 118 francs. The bourse's CAC-40 index was down 0.6 percent.

Renault's performance was helped last month by demand for its new Espace minivan and popular Megane mini-minivan, the Scenic. The spokeswoman said Renault was producing 700 Scenic models daily and had reduced delivery times to between six and eight weeks from more than 10 a month ago.
